Supply, Demand, and Equilibrium

The competitive equilibrium is where demand P=A−QP = A - QP=A−Q meets supply P=C+QP = C + QP=C+Q. Raise the per-unit tax ttt and a wedge opens between the buyer and seller prices, splitting consumer surplus, producer surplus, revenue, and deadweight loss in real time.

Q∗=A−CB+D,P∗=A−BQ∗Q^* = \frac{A-C}{B+D}, \qquad P^* = A - BQ^*Q∗=B+DA−C​,P∗=A−BQ∗
DWL=t(Q∗−Qt)2DWL = \frac{t(Q^* - Q_t)}{2}DWL=2t(Q∗−Qt​)​

Examples & Exercises

In a market with demand P=10−QP = 10 - QP=10−Q and supply P=2+QP = 2 + QP=2+Q, a per-unit tax t=2t = 2t=2 is imposed. Compute by hand the equilibrium quantity, the buyer and seller prices, and the deadweight loss.

Q∗=A−CB+D,Qt=A−C−tB+DQ^* = \frac{A - C}{B + D}, \qquad Q_t = \frac{A - C - t}{B + D}Q∗=B+DA−C​,Qt​=B+DA−C−t​
DWL=t(Q∗−Qt)2DWL = \frac{t (Q^* - Q_t)}{2}DWL=2t(Q∗−Qt​)​
Show proof
  1. The no-tax equilibrium is Q∗=(10−2)/2=4Q^* = (10-2)/2 = 4Q∗=(10−2)/2=4, P∗=10−4=6P^* = 10 - 4 = 6P∗=10−4=6.
  2. After the tax the quantity is Qt=(10−2−2)/2=3Q_t = (10-2-2)/2 = 3Qt​=(10−2−2)/2=3. The seller price on the supply curve is Ps=2+3=5P_s = 2 + 3 = 5Ps​=2+3=5, the buyer price on the demand curve is Pb=10−3=7P_b = 10 - 3 = 7Pb​=10−3=7, and the gap is exactly t=2t = 2t=2.
  3. Consumer surplus is (10−7)⋅3/2=4.5(10-7)\cdot 3/2 = 4.5(10−7)⋅3/2=4.5, producer surplus is (5−2)⋅3/2=4.5(5-2)\cdot 3/2 = 4.5(5−2)⋅3/2=4.5, revenue is 2⋅3=62 \cdot 3 = 62⋅3=6. Deadweight loss is 2⋅(4−3)2=1\frac{2 \cdot (4-3)}{2} = 122⋅(4−3)​=1 — the triangle between value and cost on the lost unit. They sum to 4.5+4.5+6+1=164.5+4.5+6+1 = 164.5+4.5+6+1=16, the no-tax total surplus.
    4.5+4.5+6+1⏟DWL=164.5 + 4.5 + 6 + \underbrace{1}_{DWL} = 164.5+4.5+6+DWL1​​=16

In the same example, compute how the tax burden falls on buyers versus sellers, and explain it through the slopes of demand and supply.

Show proof
  1. The buyer burden is Pb−P∗=7−6=1P_b - P^* = 7 - 6 = 1Pb​−P∗=7−6=1 and the seller burden is P∗−Ps=6−5=1P^* - P_s = 6 - 5 = 1P∗−Ps​=6−5=1. They sum to t=2t = 2t=2.
  2. Here demand and supply have equal slope magnitudes (111), so the burden splits evenly. In general the buyer share is DB+D\frac{D}{B+D}B+DD​ and the seller share is BB+D\frac{B}{B+D}B+DB​ — the relatively inelastic (steeper) side bears more.
    buyer share=DB+D,seller share=BB+D\text{buyer share} = \frac{D}{B+D}, \qquad \text{seller share} = \frac{B}{B+D}buyer share=B+DD​,seller share=B+DB​
